To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ca, but not Mg, depresses Zn utilization and that phytate depresses Zn utilization more at low than at high Ca levels.

dietary Ca and Mg levels affect Zn utilization in phosvitin-containing diets, that Ca has a greater effect than Mg and that the effects of both elements are greater in phosvitins with higher Ca:Mg ratios.

Ca, phytate, Mg and Ca x phytate interactions all depress Zn utilization, that Ca and phytates have the strongest effects, and that bone Zn accumulation is a more sensitive criterion of the effects than weight gain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of dietary phytin (sodium phytate) levels on the utilization of zinc in the rat.
the effects of Ca, phytate and Mg on the utilization of zinc in the rat.
the effects of dietary phytates, calcium and magnesium on the bioavailability of zinc to young growing rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of dietary Ca and Mg on Zn utilization are not as great in the presence of dietary phytates as they are in their absence.
phytate and Ca interact in depressing Zn utilization and that the effects of Mg on Zn utilization are less pronounced.
Ca is more antagonistic than Mg to the utilization of Zn from phytate-containing foods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca, phytate and Mg exert their effects on Zn bioavailability through the same mechanism, i.e. by affecting the rate of Zn transfer across the intestinal mucosal barrier.
the effects of dietary Ca on Zn utilization are dependent upon the level of dietary phytic acid and that the effects of phytic acid are dependent upon the Ca content of the diet.
phytate depresses Zn utilization in the rat, that this effect is more marked at higher dietary levels of Ca and Mg, and that Ca is more effective than Mg in this connection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca is the primary dietary factor that affects Zn bioavailability in the context of phytate and that Mg has a secondary but significant effect.
phytate and Ca are antagonistic to Zn bioavailability, and Mg is antagonistic to phytate bioavailability.
the Ca level in the diet should be kept as low as possible when phytate is present.
